title: Finite-Sample Convergence inNetworked Average Reward MARL:Decentralization Pitfalls and Entropy Remedies

paper.title: Finite-Sample Convergence in Networked Average Reward MARL: Decentralization Pitfalls and Entropy Remedies
paper.abstract:
Abstract We study the problem of average reward Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) where agents interact within a network. Each agent in the network conducts local updates with information within its k k -hop neighborhood and collaboratively maximizes the overall reward of the entire network. We first provide impossibility results in achieving convergence to the global optimal joint policies in our setting.
These impossibility results highlight the challenges of decentralized learning with local information in multi-agent systems, namely the issues of multiagency , where each agent independently optimizes its policy, and partial observability , where agents have limited visibility into the global state. Given these challenges which indicate that decentralized policy optimization can generally be certified only up to stationarity, we provide finite-sample convergence guarantees for a decentralized actor-critic algorithm with linear function approximation that converges to an approximate stationary point with small gradient norm. To overcome such impossibility results, we further show that adding fixed-state entropy regularization reshapes the objective landscape which leads to even stronger global convergence guarantees for our proposed actor-critic algorithm.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has been a practically important regime for training real-world cooperative multi-agent systems, with applications ranging from autonomous driving ( Dinneweth et al., 2022 ) , energy systems ( Keren et al., 2024 ) and robotics ( Orr and Dutta, 2023 ) . When scaling up the number of agents for better cooperation in more complex multi-agent systems, we are faced with a problem known as the curse of dimensionality : the joint state-action space scales exponentially in the number of agents, making centralized value estimation, policy optimization, and exploration statistically and computationally intractable ( Kearns and Koller, 1999 ; Zhang et al., 2021a ; Shi et al., 2025 ) . To make multi-agent systems more scalable, one promising approach is to leverage the problem structure. Among various different structures, a line of work considering networked MARL, where agents are associated within a network and only interact with neighboring agents, has gained much attention ( Qu et al., 2022 ; Qu et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ) . Such networked structure can be used to model various multi-agent systems including social networks ( Llas et al., 2003 ) , communication networks ( Zocca, 2019 ) and smart transportation ( Zhang and Pavone, 2016 ) . Leveraging the local interaction structure, Qu et al. (2022) formulated an exponential decay property, which formulates the system identity that the impact of an agent decays exponentially in the distance within the network. Using this property, agents can infer the global Q Q function and update its policy based only on the information available nearby ( Qu et al., 2022 ; Qu et al., 2020 ) , thereby making network MARL more scalable. Despite this breadth, prior analyses leave two gaps. First, the optimality of stationary points of policy-gradient objective has been extensively characterized in single-agent settings across a variety of MDP formulations ( Kumar et al., 2025 ; Mei et al., 2020 ; Even-Dar et al., 2009 ; Murthy and Srikant, 2023 ) , whereas analogous insights for networked average-reward MARL—where agents are constrained to localized policies and update with nearby information—have not been developed. Second, existing convergence guarantees in this setting are largely tabular convergence to stationary points—the policy gradient norm vanishes in the limit ( Qu et al., 2022 ; Qu et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Finite-time bounds that characterize the suboptimality of the policy as a function of the number of samples used for training, and that expose how the localization error from k k -hop truncation, the function-approximation error from the feature class, and the statistical TD error from finite samples interact, have not been established for networked average-reward MARL. This motivates the two central questions of this paper: Are global convergence guarantees achievable under decentralized localized learning? How do localization, function approximation, and the number of samples used for learning interact in the policy-based analyses of average-reward networked MARL?

sections.heading: Our contributions.
sections.text: We address these questions through three main contributions. 1. We identify Multiagency and Partial Observability —two intrinsic structural obstructions to global convergence under unregularized decentralized learning. For multiagency, we show through Example 2 that while ergodicity of the induced Markov chain guarantees global optimality of every stationary point of policy gradient in single-agent RL ( Kumar et al., 2025 ) , this guarantee fails once the joint policy is constrained to be a product of local policies, even in a fully cooperative, fully observable, ergodic MDP. For partial observability, Example 3 shows that when the individual policies cannot depend on the global state, a vanishing local policy gradient need not even certify a notion of unilateral optimality: the stationary point can have strictly positive Nash gap, i.e., at least one agent has a profitable deviation given the others’ policies fixed. These two examples reflect broader coordination and local-information challenges in cooperative MARL, and motivate why our unregularized guarantees are stated in terms of stationarity. 2. We connect network localization with linear function approximation and derive finite-sample guarantees for the resulting actor-critic method. We observe that a k k -hop tabular critic is simply a linear approximation to the global Q Q -function, with features that group together global state-action pairs indistinguishable from agent i’s local view. This perspective allows each agent to use a compact linear critic on its k-hop neighborhood, rather than maintaining an exponentially large local table. It also reveals a clear tradeoff: larger neighborhoods reduce localization bias, but require richer features to avoid approximation error. Using this localized-linear critic, we prove finite-sample stationarity of unregularized decentralized actor-critic. The resulting bound groups the error into a finite-sample learning term, which captures critic tracking, Markovian sampling, and actor-critic coupling, plus two structural approximation terms: feature approximation and network localization. 3. We show that adding strong fixed-state entropy regularization can restore global convergence. The regularized algorithm adds an analytic local entropy-gradient correction while leaving the reward critic unchanged. Theorem 5 gives finite-time global convergence for the fixed-state entropy objective under the entropy-dominance and uniform-exploration conditions. In contrast to the unregularized case, the regularized result admits convergence to the globally optimal regularized objective function, and improves the best-iterate guarantee to a stronger last-iterate. Additionally, the regularized suboptimality contracts geometrically up to the statistical, approximation, and localization errors.

sections.heading: 3 Impossibility Results
sections.text: If we use a centralized policy that has access to the global state and directly optimizes the joint global actions, the problem reduces to a single-agent average-reward RL problem, where policy gradient has global convergence guarantee to the optimal objective function J ∗ ​ ( θ ) J^{*}(\theta) ( Kumar et al., 2025 ) . However, prior works ( Qu et al., 2022 ; Qu et al., 2020 ) that adopted a localized policy ( π θ i \pi_{\theta_{i}} only depends on the local state s i s_{i} ) were only able to achieve convergence results in terms of the gradient norm ‖ ∇ J ​ ( θ ) ‖ \|\nabla J(\theta)\| , instead of the more desirable global optimality J ∗ ​ ( θ ) J^{*}(\theta) itself. To investigate whether global convergence is attainable under this localized learning setting, notice that when each agent i i has a local policy π θ i \pi_{\theta_{i}} that only depends on its local state s i s_{i} , the average-reward policy gradient theorem (Lemma 35 ) provides a useful lens for the decentralized policy optimization objective: For a tabular softmax local policy and every ( s ¯ i , a ¯ i ) ∈ 𝒮 i × 𝒜 i (\bar{s}_{i},\bar{a}_{i})\in\mathcal{S}_{i}\times\mathcal{A}_{i} , ∂ J ⁡ ( θ ) ∂ θ i ​ ( s ¯ i , a ¯ i ) \displaystyle\frac{\partial J(\theta)}{\partial\theta_{i}(\bar{s}_{i},\bar{a}_{i})} = ∑ s − i ∈ 𝒮 − i d θ ​ ( s ¯ i , s − i ) ​ π θ i ​ ( a ¯ i | s ¯ i ) ​ A ¯ i θ ​ ( ( s ¯ i , s − i ) , a ¯ i ) , \displaystyle=\sum_{s_{-i}\in\mathcal{S}_{-i}}d^{\theta}(\bar{s}_{i},s_{-i})\pi_{\theta_{i}}(\bar{a}_{i}|\bar{s}_{i})\bar{A}_{i}^{\theta}((\bar{s}_{i},s_{-i}),\bar{a}_{i}), (10) where A ¯ i θ ​ ( s g , a i ) \displaystyle\text{where}\quad\bar{A}_{i}^{\theta}(s_{g},a_{i}) : = ∑ a − i ∈ 𝒜 − i π θ − i ​ ( a − i | s − i ) ​ Q θ ​ ( s g , a i , a − i ) − V θ ​ ( s g ) . \displaystyle:=\sum_{a_{-i}\in\mathcal{A}_{-i}}\pi_{\theta_{-i}}(a_{-i}|s_{-i})Q^{\theta}(s_{g},a_{i},a_{-i})-V^{\theta}(s_{g}). (11) Here A ¯ i θ ​ ( s g , a i ) \bar{A}_{i}^{\theta}(s_{g},a_{i}) is the advantage of forcing agent i i to take action a i a_{i} while averaging over the other agents’ current actions. Here V θ ​ ( s g ) ≔ ∑ a g π θ ​ ( a g | s g ) ​ Q θ ​ ( s g , a g ) V^{\theta}(s_{g})\coloneqq\sum_{a_{g}}\pi_{\theta}(a_{g}|s_{g})Q^{\theta}(s_{g},a_{g}) and d θ ​ ( s g ) ≔ ∑ a g ν θ ​ ( s g , a g ) . d^{\theta}(s_{g})\coloneqq\sum_{a_{g}}\nu^{\theta}(s_{g},a_{g}). Based on the averaged advantage A ¯ i θ ​ ( s g , a i ) \bar{A}_{i}^{\theta}(s_{g},a_{i}) , the policy gradient ( 10 ) further averages over the state s − i s_{-i} of other agents, which the policy of agent i i doesn’t have access to. Averaging over other agents’ actions and states provides a coarse-grained gradient signal for each local action a ¯ i \bar{a}_{i} under local state s ¯ i \bar{s}_{i} . In this section we show that due to the averaging in ( 10 ) and ( 11 ), global optimality cannot be guaranteed in general for decentralized product-policy actor methods, and provide two distinct sources of suboptimality— multiagency and partial observability .

sections.heading: Challenge 1: Multiagency.
sections.text: Multiagency is the scenario where each agent maintains and updates its own policy in a decentralized manner. sections.text: Let p := π 1 ​ ( a ∣ s ) p:=\pi_{1}(a\mid s) and q := π 2 ​ ( a ∣ s ) q:=\pi_{2}(a\mid s) . Under the product policy, we have J ⁡ ( p , q ) = 2 ​ p ​ q + ( 1 − p ) ​ ( 1 − q ) = 1 − p − q + 3 ​ p ​ q J(p,q)=2pq+(1-p)(1-q)=1-p-q+3pq and ∇ J ​ ( p , q ) = ( − 1 + 3 ​ q , − 1 + 3 ​ p ) \nabla J(p,q)=(-1+3q,\,-1+3p) . sections.heading: Centralized learning.
sections.text: For the centralized single-agent formulation with joint-action space 𝒰 := { ( a , a ) , ( a , b ) , ( b , a ) , ( b , b ) } \mathcal{U}:=\{(a,a),(a,b),(b,a),(b,b)\} and policy x ∈ Δ ⁡ ( 𝒰 ) x\in\Delta(\mathcal{U}) , the same objective is linear: J ⁡ ( x ) = 2 ​ x a ​ a + x b ​ b J(x)=2x_{aa}+x_{bb} . Therefore it is simply a multi-armed bandit problem and there are no suboptimal local optima. For the sake of brevity, Example 2 is not fully consistent with the networked MDP setting. This does not invalidate the earlier observation regarding suboptimal convergence, as we show an example that is fully compatible with our framework in Appendix C . Example 2 illustrates that even in a fully cooperative and fully observable setting, decentralized learning with product policies can converge to a suboptimal local optimum. From the viewpoint of ( 11 ), each actor coordinate measures only a unilateral action change while the other agents keep their current policies. Near ( p , q ) = ( 0 , 0 ) (p,q)=(0,0) , such a unilateral move mainly creates mismatched low-reward actions, while the coordinated improvement to ( 1 , 1 ) (1,1) is invisible to a single-agent gradient. This product-policy geometry turns the centralized linear objective into a non-concave landscape, and decentralized gradient dynamics can then get stuck at its suboptimal local optima. This multiagency challenge is fundamental to decentralized learning: Once the global policy is constrained to be products of local policies in independent learning, one should not expect global optimality of policy gradient in general. Instead, one could at best hope for achieving optimality unilaterally, which asserts that each agent is acting optimally assuming other agents are fixed. To measure this unilateral optimality, for a policy class Π ¯ i \overline{\Pi}_{i} available to agent i i , define the agent-wise Nash gap : NashGap i ​ ( θ ) := sup π i ′ ∈ Π ¯ i J ⁡ ( π i ′ , θ − i ) − J ⁡ ( θ ) . \mathrm{NashGap}_{i}(\theta):=\sup_{\pi_{i}^{\prime}\in\overline{\Pi}_{i}}J(\pi_{i}^{\prime},\theta_{-i})-J(\theta). (12) Here J ⁡ ( π i ′ , θ − i ) J(\pi_{i}^{\prime},\theta_{-i}) is the average reward obtained when agent i i unilaterally switches to π i ′ \pi_{i}^{\prime} while all other agents keep their current policies. Thus NashGap i ​ ( θ ) = 0 \mathrm{NashGap}_{i}(\theta)=0 means that agent i i has no profitable unilateral deviation within its admissible local policy class, and ∑ i NashGap i ​ ( θ ) \sum_{i}\mathrm{NashGap}_{i}(\theta) measures the aggregate incentive for decentralized deviation. Although this does not rule out local optima such as Example 2 , it is the desirable convergence certificate in the decentralized setting: It guarantees that the product policy is locally stable against any single agent’s policy improvement.

sections.heading: 5 Numerical Illustration
sections.text: The error decomposition ( 9 ) suggests a qualitative tradeoff: a larger critic radius reveals neighbor information but makes a fixed-dimensional representation compress a larger neighborhood. We illustrate this with a finite-state system of interacting maintenance units. Each unit has a binary health state, chooses a binary intervention action, and records its previous action as a one-step memory variable. Its local reward favors healthy operation while penalizing intervention, and its health transition depends on its own state and action together with the health and previous actions of adjacent units. We test paths with N ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 } N\in\{8,16,32,64\} agents and square grids with side length L ∈ { 3 , 4 , 6 , 8 } L\in\{3,4,6,8\} , hence N ∈ { 9 , 16 , 36 , 64 } N\in\{9,16,36,64\} agents. We sweep k ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 } k\in\{0,1,2,3\} and pairwise-hashed feature dimensions d i ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 } d_{i}\in\{4,8,16,32,64\} , with a tabular critic for comparison. Each cell uses 3,000 3{,}000 training steps and a fresh 300 300 -step greedy evaluation; each plotted point pools the four listed sizes and three seeds. Full protocol details and additional sweeps are in Appendix H . Figure 3: Greedy reward per agent versus k k (a,b) and d i d_{i} (c,d). Means pool 12 runs (four sizes, three seeds each); bars show descriptive normal-approximation 95% confidence intervals. At d i = 16 d_{i}=16 , paths score 0.676 ± 0.002 0.676\pm 0.002 at k = 1 k=1 but 0.392 ± 0.148 0.392\pm 0.148 at k = 3 k=3 , while grid k = 2 , 3 k=2,3 stay near 0.058 0.058 ; all positive radii reach about 0.676 0.676 by d i = 32 d_{i}=32 on paths or d i = 64 d_{i}=64 on grids. Tabular stays near 0.058 0.058 on grids and peaks at only 0.369 ± 0.006 0.369\pm 0.006 on paths. Under the same trajectory budget, the tabular critic fails to learn effectively, showing that function approximation is necessary in this tested growing-neighborhood regime. Thus, larger neighborhoods help only when encoded: grid k = 2 , 3 k=2,3 match k = 1 k=1 only at d i = 64 d_{i}=64 , and path k = 3 k=3 matches k = 1 k=1 by d i = 32 d_{i}=32 . Limitations and Future Work. A key limitation is that our guarantees rely on the exponential decay property in the network: they apply only to settings where each agent’s state transition is influenced only by its immediate neighbors, so relaxing this local weak-dependence structure is an important future direction. Fixed-state entropy regularization should also be viewed as a remedy rather than a universal fix, as our global convergence guarantee requires the entropy to be strong. Future work includes identifying different policy classes (in addition to localized policies) and structural assumptions on the global transition kernel of the multi-agent MDPs under which decentralized policy-optimization methods have more favorable landscapes and may admit either global convergence guarantees or finite-time convergence to zero Nash gap.

sections.heading: Appendix B Related Work
sections.text: In this section we provide a detailed discussion on related work.

sections.heading: Networked multi-agent reinforcement learning.
sections.text: Our work lies in the line of literature that designs scalable multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms for networked systems. Within this domain, we especially follow the framework of Qu et al. [2022] that leverages spatial correlation decay to achieve provable convergence guarantees. Qu et al. [2020] extended this local interaction structure of networks to establish an exponential spatial decay property for policy gradients in the average-reward setting. Lin et al. [2021] further considered environments with stochastic network transitions, demonstrating that spatial decay properties can be leveraged to bound approximation errors independently of the total network size. Building upon this framework, Zhang et al. [2023] considered a wider class of policies that depends on all states in the k k -hop neighborhood, and proved the convergence of localized policy iteration to a globally optimal policy that potentially depends on the entire global state. Furthermore, Zhou et al. [2023] extended this fully cooperative framework to a class of networked Markov potential games, and established finite-time global convergence rates for localized actor-critic algorithms, and more recently, Ren et al. [2025] leveraged spectral representations of the underlying network topology to efficiently compress high-dimensional state and action spaces. Faizal et al. [2026] study discounted graph-structured MDPs with local rewards and transitions. Under influence-decay conditions, they establish optimal-policy approximation guarantees for cooperative policies. Their multi-agent construction selects a joint action by maximizing a sum of neighborhood-dependent Q Q -factors. The resulting policy can use neighboring states and coordinated action selection. Their multi-agent result establishes existence of a good cooperative policy, while efficient computation of its surrogate remains open; their single-active-agent setting also admits constructive algorithms. Meanwhile, we note that there are other models for the networked MARL problem that models the interaction between agents differently. Zhang et al. [2018] first proposed the framework of networked multi-agent MDP without considering localization of policy and Q Q functions in the network. Liu et al. [2026] studied local convergence distributed policy gradient and actor-critic in the discounted setting. Despite this progress, finite-time convergence results in average-reward networked MARL leveraging the spatial decay properties has never been established.

sections.heading: Average-reward reinforcement learning.
sections.text: Classical dynamic-programming treatments of average-cost MDPs are given in Bertsekas [2007] . More recently, finite-time policy-optimization guarantees have been developed for single-agent average-reward MDPs, including vanilla policy-gradient methods Kumar et al. [2025] and natural-policy-gradient or mirror-descent-type methods [ Murthy and Srikant, 2023 , Grosof et al., 2025 , Even-Dar et al., 2009 ] . Asymptotic analysis of actor critic algorithms comprising of both policy gradient and natural policy gradient goes back to Konda and Tsitsiklis [1999] , Bhatnagar et al. [2009] . Finite-sample analyses of average-reward TD and Q-learning were developed by Zhang et al. [2021b] , and finite-time actor-critic guarantees were later obtained under two-timescale stepsizes by Wu et al. [2020] and under single-timescale Markovian sampling by Chen and Zhao [2023] . Our critic analysis builds on these standard average-reward TD and stochastic-approximation ideas, but applies them to a collection of localized network critics. These results have been used to derive finite-sample complexity guarantees for popular algorithms such as natural policy gradient [ Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2019 , Murthy et al., 2023 , Murthy et al., 2024 ] in the single agent setting. Average-reward MARL has also been studied in fully decentralized communication-based settings. Hairi et al. [2022] prove finite-time convergence for a consensus-based fully decentralized actor-critic algorithm in cooperative average-reward MARL, where agents communicate local TD-error information to estimate a global actor direction. Hairi et al. [2024] study the related policy-evaluation problem and show that multiple local TD steps between communication rounds can reduce communication complexity. These works address decentralized communication and consensus in average-reward MARL. Our focus is different: we study networked MDPs with spatially local state-action information, where each agent uses a k k -hop localized critic rather than communicating to learn a common global critic. This leads to explicit localization and function-approximation error floors in the actor-critic convergence bound.

sections.heading: Other related work.
sections.text: In addition to networked and average-reward settings, we also briefly acknowledge a wider body of literature. Mei et al. [2020] established global convergence rates for softmax policy gradients for bandits and discounted RL. Zhang et al. [2022] provided global convergence results for softmax (natural) policy gradients for a class of Markov potential games. DeWeese and Qu [2026] optimize over the full simplex of distributions on a restricted deterministic policy class in discounted MDPs. Their evaluation samples a deterministic policy, holds it fixed for several time steps, and then resamples. Under smoothness, their exact-gradient guarantees control the expected performance of a final sampled deterministic policy relative to the best deterministic member of that class, with a residual decreasing exponentially in the temporal horizon. Their multi-step horizon measures time rather than graph distance. Liu et al. [2022] studies sample complexity in partially observable Marko games, proposing the Optimism and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (OMLE) algorithm to establish polynomial sample complexity bounds for learning approximate Nash, correlated, and coarse correlated equilibria under weak revealability assumptions. Hong et al. [2023] provided finite-sample (non-asymptotic) convergence guarantees for policy gradients utilizing history-dependent policies in continuous-space POMDPs. Forkel et al. [2026] investigated high entropy in Dec-POMDPs and found that high fixed-state entropy regularization helps the convergence of policy gradient methods to symmetry equivariant policies. While these work share somewhat similar high-level intuition as ours, the specific settings that they consider differ significantly from our networked MDP setting.

sections.heading: Appendix C Example of Policy Gradient Converging to a Suboptimal Stationary Point
sections.text: We next construct a cooperative two-agent example showing that even under ergodicity, policy gradient with product policies can converge to a suboptimal local optimum in policy space. In contrast to Example 2 , in this setting the reward assigned to each agent is a function solely of its own state and action, while the transition dynamics remain jointly coupled across the two agents, thereby preserving the interaction structure central to the problem formulation considered in this work.

sections.heading: Appendix E Convergence Proof without Regularization
sections.text: In this section we present the convergence proof of the decentralized actor-critic algorithm without regularization. We separate the proof into three steps: The convergence of the critic, the convergence of the actor, and the overall convergence.

sections.heading: E.1 Convergence of the Critic
sections.text: This section establishes finite-time convergence of the critic component of the decentralized actor-critic algorithm.

sections.heading: Proof roadmap.
sections.text: The critic proof has two layers: fixed-policy approximation and moving-target stability. Lemma 2 first resolves the average-reward constant-shift ambiguity by selecting a unique normalized projected Bellman fixed point, and Lemma 3 gives the contraction coefficients that make this fixed point stable. Proposition 2 supplies the constrained-projection identities used by Lemma 4 ,which bounds the error of the localized tabular projected fixed point relative to the true local Q Q -function in terms of restricted projected Bellman gap of the global transition matrix. Lemma 5 then proves fixed-policy TD contraction, and Theorem 6 converts that contraction plus the approximation floor into finite-time local and global value-function bounds. Finally, Lemma 6 , Lemma 7 , Lemma 8 , and Corollary 139 show that the same critic tracking remains controlled when the actor moves. Proposition 2 supplies the constrained-projection identities used by Lemma 4, which bounds the error of the localized tabular projected fixed point relative to the true local Q Q -function, i.e., the spatial localization part of the approximation floor.

sections.text: The localization matrix ϕ i \phi_{i} has a very specific structure. It is a { 0 , 1 } \{0,1\} -valued matrix of size ϕ i ∈ { 0 , 1 } | 𝒮 g × 𝒜 g | × | 𝒮 i k × 𝒜 i k | , \phi_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal{S}_{g}\times\mathcal{A}_{g}|\times|\mathcal{S}_{i}^{k}\times\mathcal{A}_{i}^{k}|}, whose rows are indexed by global state-action pairs and whose columns are indexed by local state-action pairs on the k k -hop neighborhood of agent i i . For a global state-action pair x g ∈ 𝒮 g × 𝒜 g x_{g}\in\mathcal{S}_{g}\times\mathcal{A}_{g} and a local state-action pair x i k ∈ 𝒮 i k × 𝒜 i k x_{i}^{k}\in\mathcal{S}_{i}^{k}\times\mathcal{A}_{i}^{k} , the entry of ϕ i \phi_{i} is given by [ ϕ i ] x g , x i k = { x i k = Proj N i k ( x g ) } , [\phi_{i}]_{x_{g},x_{i}^{k}}=\mathbf{1}\!\left\{x_{i}^{k}=\mathrm{Proj}_{N_{i}^{k}}(x_{g})\right\}, where Proj N i k ​ ( x g ) \mathrm{Proj}_{N_{i}^{k}}(x_{g}) denotes the restriction of the global state-action pair x g x_{g} to the k k -hop neighborhood N i k N_{i}^{k} of agent i i . Thus, each row of ϕ i \phi_{i} has exactly one nonzero entry, and that nonzero entry is equal to 1 1 . Indeed, every global state-action pair has a unique projection onto the local k k -hop neighborhood. In this sense, ϕ i \phi_{i} precisely encodes the mapping from the global state-action space to the local state-action space. Also, different columns of ϕ i \phi_{i} have disjoint supports, and each column is nonzero. Therefore, the columns are linearly independent, so ϕ i \phi_{i} has full column rank. Equivalently, for any local tabular vector q i ∈ ℝ | 𝒮 i k × 𝒜 i k | q_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}_{i}^{k}\times\mathcal{A}_{i}^{k}|} , the lifted vector ϕ i ​ q i ∈ ℝ | 𝒮 g × 𝒜 g | \phi_{i}q_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{S}_{g}\times\mathcal{A}_{g}|} is given by ( ϕ i ​ q i ) ​ ( x g ) = q i ​ ( Proj N i k ​ ( x g ) ) . E.2 Convergence of the Actor
sections.text: We now prove the actor-side stationarity estimate for the unregularized objective. The proof is written so that it can be coupled with the single-timescale moving-target critic recursion from the preceding critic subsection. The conclusion is a bound on the policy-gradient norm; no unregularized global optimality or Nash-gap conclusion is used in this subsection.

sections.heading: Proof roadmap.
sections.text: The actor proof first identifies the exact gradient target and then bounds each source of bias around it. Lemma 9 and Lemma 10 give the score identities, score bounds, and kernel Lipschitz constants needed for all actor estimates, serving as the regularity conditions for the actor proof throughout. Lemma 11 turns delayed Markovian samples into current-stationary expectations through leveraging the mixing properties of the induced Markov chain. Lemma 12 and Lemma 13 quantify the localization bias caused by using only nearby critics. Lemma 14 , Lemma 15 , and Lemma 16 control smoothness, critic-induced gradient error, and stochastic variance respectively; Lemma 17 combines these estimates into a one-step ascent recursion. Proposition 3 telescopes this drift into a stationarity bound. The auxiliary comparison facts, Lemma 18 and Lemma 19 , are the formal comparison counterparts of the partial-observability challenge: the first rewrites unilateral improvement through the one-agent averaged advantage, and the second explains when a softmax-gradient bound can or cannot control the Nash gap. Theorem 7 then combines the actor and critic estimates into the final unregularized finite-time result. sections.heading: Algorithmic template.
sections.text: The fixed-state entropy-regularized method is the regularized actor-update branch of Algorithm 1 ; this branch adds only the analytic entropy-gradient term to the actor update and leaves the reward-only TD critic unchanged.

sections.heading: Proof roadmap.
sections.text: The regularized proof reuses the critic analysis from Subsection E.1 , because fixed-state entropy modifies only the actor objective and leaves the reward-only TD target unchanged. Lemma 20 records the actor-side boundedness, Lipschitz, and localization consequences needed after adding entropy, and Lemma 21 identifies the exact local entropy-gradient blocks. Lemma 22 , Lemma 23 , and Lemma 24 then repeat the unregularized actor logic for the regularized direction: control gradient bias, control variance, and prove one-step ascent for J ι , ω J_{\iota,\omega} . Theorem 8 telescopes this drift into finite-time stationarity, Theorem 9 converts stationarity to a regularized value-gap bound under a PL condition, and Corollary 2 translates that bound back to the unregularized objective. The strong-entropy route in Subsection F.3 is the conditional argument showing that fixed-state entropy can turn the product-policy landscape into one satisfying a PL inequality when its negative curvature dominates the positive curvature of the unregularized objective on the explored region. Lemma 25 bounds the direct-policy curvature of J J on Π 0 \Pi_{0} by L ¯ J \overline{L}_{J} . Lemma 26 combines this curvature bound with the entropy Hessian lower bound from the positive state-weight condition to prove direct-policy strong concavity whenever ι ​ ω min > L ¯ J \iota\omega_{\min}>\overline{L}_{J} . Lemma 27 converts that direct-policy strong concavity into a PL inequality for the tangent direct-policy gradient G Π ​ ( π ) G_{\Pi}(\pi) . Lemma 28 then transfers this direct-policy PL inequality to the softmax-logit gradient using the exploration lower bound δ \delta , which is the PL condition required by Theorem 9 . Finally, Theorem 10 plugs this verified PL constant into the finite-time recursion to obtain the stated strong-entropy global convergence consequence.

sections.heading: F.1 Convergence of the Critic
sections.text: The fixed-state entropy objective analyzed in this section does not change the reward process or the Poisson equation that the critic estimates. The regularized objective is obtained by adding to the actor objective a deterministic function of the current local policy tables. Consequently the critic continues to estimate the reward-only local action-value functions Q i θ Q_{i}^{\theta} defined in the preliminaries, with the same TD target r i ​ ( s i ​ ( t ) , a i ​ ( t ) ) − μ i t + ψ i ​ ( s i k ​ ( t + 1 ) , a i k ​ ( t + 1 ) ) ⊤ ​ w i t − ψ i ​ ( s i k ​ ( t ) , a i k ​ ( t ) ) ⊤ ​ w i t . r_{i}(s_{i}(t),a_{i}(t))-\mu_{i}^{t}+\psi_{i}(s_{i}^{k}(t+1),a_{i}^{k}(t+1))^{\top}w_{i}^{t}-\psi_{i}(s_{i}^{k}(t),a_{i}^{k}(t))^{\top}w_{i}^{t}. No new critic convergence proof is needed for this fixed-state regularization. All critic tracking bounds from the unregularized proof, including the definition of 𝒱 t \mathcal{V}_{t} in ( 145 ), apply verbatim.

sections.text: This section provides a numerical illustration of the interaction between the critic neighborhood radius k k and the dimension D = d i D=d_{i} of a linear representation. The experiment is designed to visualize the structural tradeoff in the bounds that a larger neighborhood can reduce omitted-information error while making a fixed-dimensional critic harder to fit.

sections.heading: Feature construction and updates.
sections.text: Neighborhood observations concatenate ( h j , m j ) (h_{j},m_{j}) in increasing node-index order. Critic keys append the focal action and the number of active immediate neighbors, capped at four; this count is retained even at k = 0 k=0 . For a token sequence q q , the first four feature coordinates are initialized as 1 1 , mean ⁡ ( q ) / 4 \operatorname{mean}(q)/4 , max ⁡ ( q ) / 4 \max(q)/4 , and min ⁡ ( 1 , | q | / 32 ) \min(1,|q|/32) . Deterministic signed hashes add individual-token contributions; pairwise features also hash adjacent tokens in this sequence. Critic features additionally hash the action, count, and their interaction. Hashes use the remaining coordinates for D > 4 D>4 and share the three non-bias coordinates for D = 4 D=4 ; the resulting vector is normalized to unit Euclidean norm. The exact integer mixer and token weights are specified in src/sampled_actor_critic.py in the accompanying source package. Initial health and memory coordinates are independent Bernoulli ( 1 / 2 ) (1/2) draws. Linear actor entries start as independent 0.01 ​ 𝒩 ​ ( 0 , 1 ) 0.01\,\mathcal{N}(0,1) draws; critics and average-reward estimates start at zero. Each transition updates critics and then actors sequentially by agent index, with average-reward stepsize β \beta . The actor signal combines the neighborhood mean TD error with the mean critic value minus its counterfactual baseline. Linear critic weights are projected onto the Euclidean ball of radius C w C_{w} , and actor entries are clipped to [ − C θ , C θ ] [-C_{\theta},C_{\theta}] . The tabular baseline instead uses per-agent critic tables and local plus shared actor-logit tables, splitting each actor update equally between the latter two. Its logits use the same Gaussian initialization, unseen critic entries start at zero, and critic entries are clipped individually to [ − C w , C w ] [-C_{w},C_{w}] .

sections.heading: Environment selection and aggregation.
sections.text: The environment was selected to illustrate the tradeoff. Calibration screened five parameter settings on the representative graphs, using seed 0 0 , 800 800 training steps, and 120 120 evaluation steps. For additive features at D = 8 D=8 and pairwise features at D = 8 , 16 D=8,16 , it retained the best-scoring configuration at each k k and maximized, across graph families and feature settings, the average of max ⁡ ( R 1 , R 2 ) − max ⁡ ( R 0 , R 3 ) \max(R_{1},R_{2})-\max(R_{0},R_{3}) , where R k R_{k} is the corresponding greedy reward; mean peak reward broke ties. Thus, the observed curve shape describes this selected example and need not hold across environments. Reported intervals are R ¯ ± 1.96 ​ s R / m \bar{R}\pm 1.96s_{R}/\sqrt{m} , where s R s_{R} is the sample standard deviation and m = 12 m=12 for pooled curves or m = 3 m=3 for size-specific results. They summarize variation across the included runs. An initial feature-indexing bug caused the original D = 4 D=4 runs to fail; these records are retained but excluded, and all reported D = 4 D=4 results use successful runs after the repair. Dimensions 128,256,512 128,256,512 were completed in a later extension with the same tuning and evaluation protocol.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: The pooled curves in Figure H.2 and representative entries in Table H.2 show that at small and intermediate D D , reward can first improve and then deteriorate as k k grows. For example, on grids with additive features and D = 16 D=16 , reward increases from 0.058 ± 0.003 0.058\pm 0.003 at k = 0 k=0 to 0.499 ± 0.117 0.499\pm 0.117 at k = 2 k=2 , then falls to 0.314 ± 0.146 0.314\pm 0.146 at k = 3 k=3 . The grid pairwise result at D = 8 D=8 and the path pairwise result at D = 16 D=16 show analogous reversals. The size-specific path and grid radius plots in Figures H.3 and H.5 , together with the grid values in Table H.3 , show how these reversals vary across network sizes. These patterns are consistent with an information–compression tradeoff: a positive radius makes neighbor-state information available, while a growing neighborhood must be represented with the same number of features. The precise best radius depends on the embedding and feature dimension, and the wider intervals at smaller D D indicate sensitivity to training and hash collisions. The dimension sweeps in Figures H.4 and H.6 show that increasing D D largely removes this bottleneck in the tested instances. Every positive path radius reaches approximately 0.676 0.676 by D = 32 D=32 , and every positive radius for the grid pairwise embedding reaches 0.676 ± 0.003 0.676\pm 0.003 at D = 64 D=64 . Under the same finite trajectory budget, the tabular critic remains near 0.058 0.058 for every grid radius and reaches only 0.369 ± 0.006 0.369\pm 0.006 on paths, consistent with sparse visitation of a rapidly growing local table. These comparisons illustrate why a compact linear critic can be useful even though it introduces a feature-approximation floor.

sections.heading: Relation to the theoretical framework.
sections.text: These experiments follow the same high-level localization–representation idea as Algorithm 1 : actors use local observations, critics incorporate information from a k k -hop neighborhood, rewards and transitions are locally structured, and finite-dimensional features control critic representation capacity. For scalable implementation across the tested graph families, linear actor and critic parameterizations are shared across agents, neighborhood critic quantities are averaged using a counterfactual baseline, and the actor feature map is varied together with D D . A few protocol details differ slightly: evaluation uses greedy actions rather than sampling from the stochastic softmax policy, and the tuning and main runs use partially overlapping seeds. The deterministic memory update preserves the local factorization and delayed neighbor interactions; its unit self-interaction places this instance at the boundary of, rather than strictly inside, the coefficient condition used as a sufficient route to spatial decay. These choices preserve the mechanism of interest, and the results provide a reproducible finite-state illustration of the practical localization–representation tradeoff highlighted by the analysis. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2611.04072v1 [cs.LG] 02 Nov 2026 Finite-Sample Convergence in Networked Average Reward MARL: Decentralization Pitfalls and Entropy Remedies Yizhou Zhang † † thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: California Institute of Technology Email: yzhang8@caltech.edu Yashaswini Murthy 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin Email: yashaswini.murthy@austin.utexas.edu Laixi Shi Affiliation: Johns Hopkins University Email: laixis@jhu.edu Adam Wierman Affiliation: California Institute of Technology Email: adamw@caltech.edu Abstract We study the problem of average reward Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) where agents interact within a network. Each agent in the network conducts local updates with information within its k k -hop neighborhood and collaboratively maximizes the overall reward of the entire network. We first provide impossibility results in achieving convergence to the global optimal joint policies in our setting. These impossibility results highlight the challenges of decentralized learning with local information in multi-agent systems, namely the issues of multiagency , where each agent independently optimizes its policy, and partial observability , where agents have limited visibility into the global state. Given these challenges which indicate that decentralized policy optimization can generally be certified only up to stationarity, we provide finite-sample convergence guarantees for a decentralized actor-critic algorithm with linear function approximation that converges to an approximate stationary point with small gradient norm. To overcome such impossibility results, we further show that adding fixed-state entropy regularization reshapes the objective landscape which leads to even stronger global convergence guarantees for our proposed actor-critic algorithm. 1 Introduction Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has been a practically important regime for training real-world cooperative multi-agent systems, with applications ranging from autonomous driving ( Dinneweth et al., 2022 ) , energy systems ( Keren et al., 2024 ) and robotics ( Orr and Dutta, 2023 ) . When scaling up the number of agents for better cooperation in more complex multi-agent systems, we are faced with a problem known as the curse of dimensionality : the joint state-action space scales exponentially in the number of agents, making centralized value estimation, policy optimization, and exploration statistically and computationally intractable ( Kearns and Koller, 1999 ; Zhang et al., 2021a ; Shi et al., 2025 ) . To make multi-agent systems more scalable, one promising approach is to leverage the problem structure. Among various different structures, a line of work considering networked MARL, where agents are associated within a network and only interact with neighboring agents, has gained much attention ( Qu et al., 2022 ; Qu et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ) . Such networked structure can be used to model various multi-agent systems including social networks ( Llas et al., 2003 ) , communication networks ( Zocca, 2019 ) and smart transportation ( Zhang and Pavone, 2016 ) . Leveraging the local interaction structure, Qu et al. (2022) formulated an exponential decay property, which formulates the system identity that the impact of an agent decays exponentially in the distance within the network. Using this property, agents can infer the global Q Q function and update its policy based only on the information available nearby ( Qu et al., 2022 ; Qu et al., 2020 ) , thereby making network MARL more scalable. Despite this breadth, prior analyses leave two gaps. First, the optimality of stationary points of policy-gradient objective has been extensively characterized in single-agent settings across a variety of MDP formulations ( Kumar et al., 2025 ; Mei et al., 2020 ; Even-Dar et al., 2009 ; Murthy and Srikant, 2023 ) , whereas analogous insights for networked average-reward MARL—where agents are constrained to localized policies and update with nearby information—have not been developed. Second, existing convergence guarantees in this setting are largely tabular convergence to stationary points—the policy gradient norm vanishes in the limit ( Qu et al., 2022 ; Qu et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Finite-time bounds that characterize the suboptimality of the policy as a function of the number of samples used for training, and that expose how the localization error from k k -hop truncation, the function-approximation error from the feature class, and the statistical TD error from finite samples interact, have not been established for networked average-reward MARL. This motivates the two central questions of this paper: Are global convergence guarantees achievable under decentralized localized learning? How do localization, function approximation, and the number of samples used for learning interact in the policy-based analyses of average-reward networked MARL? Our contributions. We address these questions through three main contributions. 1. We identify Multiagency and Partial Observability —two intrinsic structural obstructions to global convergence under unregularized decentralized learning. For multiagency, we show through Example 2 that while ergodicity of the induced Markov chain guarantees global optimality of every stationary point of policy gradient in single-agent RL ( Kumar et al., 2025 ) , this guarantee fails once the joint policy is constrained to be a product of local policies, even in a fully cooperative, fully observable, ergodic MDP. For partial observability, Example 3 shows that when the individual policies cannot depend on the global state, a vanishing local policy gradient need not even certify a notion of unilateral optimality: the stationary point can have strictly positive Nash gap, i.e., at least one agent has a profitable deviation given the others’ policies fixed. These two examples reflect broader coordination and local-information challenges in cooperative MARL, and motivate why our unregularized guarantees are stated in terms of stationarity. 2. We connect network localization with linear function approximation and derive finite-sample guarantees for the resulting actor-critic method. We observe that a k k -hop tabular critic is simply a linear approximation to the global Q Q -function, with features that group together global state-action pairs indistinguishable from agent i’s local view. This perspective allows each agent to use a compact linear critic on its k-hop neighborhood, rather than maintaining an exponentially large local table. It also reveals a clear tradeoff: larger neighborhoods reduce localization bias, but require richer features to avoid approximation error. Using this localized-linear critic, we prove finite-sample stationarity of unregularized decentralized actor-critic. The resulting bound groups the error into a finite-sample learning term, which captures critic tracking, Markovian sampling, and actor-critic coupling, plus two structural approximation terms: feature approximation and network localization. 3. We show that adding strong fixed-state entropy regularization can restore global convergence. The regularized algorithm adds an analytic local entropy-gradient correction while leaving the reward critic unchanged. Theorem 5 gives finite-time global convergence for the fixed-state entropy objective under the entropy-dominance and uniform-exploration conditions. In contrast to the unregularized case, the regularized result admits convergence to the globally optimal regularized objective function, and improves the best-iterate guarantee to a stronger last-iterate. Additionally, the regularized suboptimality contracts geometrically up to the statistical, approximation, and localization errors. 2 Preliminaries In this section we present our problem setup and introduce basic problem properties. 2.1 Networked Average-Reward MDP We work under the same problem setting as in Qu et al. (2020) . This product-policy geometry turns the centralized linear objective into a non-concave landscape, and decentralized gradient dynamics can then get stuck at its suboptimal local optima. This multiagency challenge is fundamental to decentralized learning: Once the global policy is constrained to be products of local policies in independent learning, one should not expect global optimality of policy gradient in general.
